name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q01 - Neural organization across diverse animal phyla

questiontext.text:
Match the organisms or animal groups in List-I with their characteristic neural organization in List-II:

List-I List-II
A. HydraI. Possesses a brain along with a number of ganglia and neural tissues
B. InsectsII. Composed of a simple network of neurons
C. VertebratesIII. Includes the brain and the spinal cord as the information processing site
D. Human Central Neural SystemIV. Possesses a more developed and complex neural system

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Animal nervous systems exhibit evolutionary progression in organizational complexity, advancing from primitive diffuse nerve nets in lower invertebrates to centralized ganglionic arrays and highly developed central neural architectures in vertebrates.

Step 2: Pairing for Hydra
Cnidarians such as Hydra represent primitive multicellular organization where the nervous system is composed simply of an uncentralized network of neurons.

Step 3: Pairing for insects
Insects demonstrate greater organizational complexity with cephalization, featuring a defined brain accompanied by paired segmental ganglia and specialized neural tissues.

Step 4: Pairing for vertebrates
Vertebrate animals possess a significantly more developed, integrated, and complex neural system compared to invertebrate phyla.

Step 5: Pairing for the human central neural system
In humans, the central neural system specifically incorporates the brain and the spinal cord, functioning as the chief command, processing, and control center.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The correct conceptual correspondence pairs Hydra with the simple network of neurons, insects with the presence of a brain and ganglia, vertebrates with the more developed neural system, and the human central neural system with the brain and spinal cord.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q02 - Functional divisions of human peripheral nerves

questiontext.text:
Match the components of the peripheral neural system in List-I with their defining functions in List-II:

List-I List-II
A. Afferent nerve fibresI. Relays regulatory impulses from the central neural system to skeletal muscles
B. Efferent nerve fibresII. Transmits impulses from peripheral tissues and organs to the central neural system
C. Somatic neural systemIII. Transmits regulatory impulses from the central neural system to involuntary organs and smooth muscles
D. Autonomic neural systemIV. Transmits regulatory impulses from the central neural system outward to peripheral tissues and organs

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The peripheral neural system comprises conducting pathways classified by impulse direction into afferent (sensory) and efferent (motor) tracts, and further divided by effector target into voluntary somatic and involuntary autonomic circuits.

Step 2: Pairing for afferent nerve fibres
Afferent nerve fibres carry sensory information centripetally, conducting impulses from sensory receptors and peripheral organs inward to the central neural system.

Step 3: Pairing for efferent nerve fibres
Efferent nerve fibres convey regulatory or motor commands centrifugally, conducting impulses outward from the central neural system to peripheral tissues and organs.

Step 4: Pairing for the somatic neural system
The somatic neural system is the voluntary efferent branch that relays motor commands from the central neural system specifically to skeletal muscles.

Step 5: Pairing for the autonomic neural system
The autonomic neural system is the involuntary efferent branch that conducts regulatory impulses from the central neural system to smooth muscles, cardiac tissue, and visceral organs.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The correct conceptual correspondence pairs afferent nerve fibres with inward transmission to the central neural system, efferent nerve fibres with outward regulatory transmission to peripheral tissues, somatic neural system with impulse relay to skeletal muscles, and autonomic neural system with conduction to involuntary organs and smooth muscles.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q03 - Morphological neuron classes and characteristic locations

questiontext.text:
Match the morphological types of neurons in List-I with their characteristic structural features and locations in List-II:

List-I List-II
A. Multipolar neuronI. Possesses one axon and one dendrite; typically found in the retina of the eye
B. Bipolar neuronII. Cell body with a single axon only; typically found during the embryonic stage
C. Unipolar neuronIII. Possesses one axon and two or more dendrites; found in the cerebral cortex
D. Synaptic knobIV. Terminal bulb-like structure of axonal branches possessing neurotransmitter vesicles

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Neurons exhibit anatomical diversity in the number of cell processes (neurites) radiating from the soma, categorizing them into multipolar, bipolar, and unipolar morphological types adapted to specialized functional sites.

Step 2: Pairing for multipolar neurons
Multipolar neurons present a soma bearing one long axon and multiple branching dendrites, predominating structurally within the cerebral cortex.

Step 3: Pairing for bipolar neurons
Bipolar neurons possess exactly two processes emerging from opposite somatic poles—one dendrite and one axon—and occur typically in specialized sensory epithelia such as the retina of the eye.

Step 4: Pairing for unipolar neurons
Unipolar neurons consist of a cell body giving rise to only a single emerging axon without dendrites, appearing primarily during early embryonic developmental stages.

Step 5: Pairing for synaptic knob
The synaptic knob is the bulbous dilation at the terminal tip of each axonal branch that stores synaptic vesicles filled with neurotransmitter molecules.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The correct conceptual correspondence pairs multipolar neurons with one axon and multiple dendrites in the cerebral cortex, bipolar neurons with one axon and one dendrite in the retina, unipolar neurons with a single axon in embryonic stages, and synaptic knob with the vesicle-containing terminal bulb.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q04 - Structural features of myelinated unmyelinated axons

questiontext.text:
Match the nerve fibre structures in List-I with their anatomical descriptions and distributions in List-II:

List-I List-II
A. Schwann cellsI. Uninsulated gaps occurring between two adjacent myelin sheaths along an axon
B. Nodes of RanvierII. Enclosed by a Schwann cell that does not form a sheath; found in autonomous and somatic systems
C. Myelinated nerve fibresIII. Glial cells that envelop nerve fibres and form myelin sheaths around axons
D. Unmyelinated nerve fibresIV. Axons enveloped by myelin sheaths; typically found in spinal and cranial nerves

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Axons in the peripheral nervous system are organized into myelinated and unmyelinated configurations depending on the nature of their association with supportive glial Schwann cells.

Step 2: Pairing for Schwann cells
Schwann cells are specialized peripheral glial cells that envelop axonal cylinders, wrapping concentric membrane layers to form insulating myelin sheaths.

Step 3: Pairing for nodes of Ranvier
Nodes of Ranvier are the bare, unmyelinated nodal gaps occurring periodically along an axon between adjacent myelin sheaths.

Step 4: Pairing for myelinated nerve fibres
Myelinated nerve fibres possess a multi-layered lipid myelin sheath and are prominently distributed within cranial and spinal nerves to enable rapid impulse conduction.

Step 5: Pairing for unmyelinated nerve fibres
Unmyelinated nerve fibres are enclosed within the cytoplasm of Schwann cells without forming concentric myelin wraps, commonly residing in autonomic and somatic neural pathways.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The correct conceptual correspondence pairs Schwann cells with glial sheath formation, nodes of Ranvier with gaps between adjacent sheaths, myelinated fibres with presence in spinal and cranial nerves, and unmyelinated fibres with Schwann cell enclosure without myelin in autonomous and somatic systems.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q05 - Biochemical factors maintaining resting axonal potential

questiontext.text:
Match the electrochemical properties of a resting axon in List-I with their physiological descriptions in List-II:

List-I List-II
A. Resting axonal membrane permeabilityI. Comparatively more permeable to potassium ions and nearly impermeable to sodium ions
B. Axoplasmic macromolecular contentII. Contains high concentration of negatively charged proteins impermeable to the membrane
C. Sodium-potassium ATPase pumpIII. Actively transports 3 sodium ions outward for every 2 potassium ions into the cell
D. Resting membrane polarityIV. Possesses a net positive charge on the outer surface and a negative charge on the inner surface

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The resting potential of a neuron reflects an asymmetric steady-state charge and ionic distribution maintained across the axolemma by selective passive leakage and active ion transport.

Step 2: Pairing for resting axonal membrane permeability
In the unexcited resting state, open leak channels make the axonal membrane significantly more permeable to potassium ions while remaining nearly impermeable to sodium ions.

Step 3: Pairing for axoplasmic macromolecular content
The intracellular axoplasm contains an abundance of large, negatively charged proteins that cannot diffuse across the impermeable plasma membrane.

Step 4: Pairing for the sodium-potassium ATPase pump
The electrogenic pump consumes cellular ATP to transport 3 sodium ions out of the axoplasm in exchange for 2 potassium ions imported into the cell.

Step 5: Pairing for resting membrane polarity
Differential ion distribution combined with active pumping establishes a polarized state where the outer membrane face is positively charged while the inner surface is negatively charged.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The correct conceptual correspondence pairs resting permeability with high potassium and low sodium permeability, axoplasmic content with impermeant negative proteins, the sodium-potassium pump with active transport of 3 sodium out for 2 potassium in, and resting polarity with positive outer and negative inner charges.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q06 - Phases of action potential and conduction

questiontext.text:
Match the electrophysiological events of nerve impulse conduction in List-I with their underlying mechanisms in List-II:

List-I List-II
A. Stimulus application at excited siteI. Flows from excited site to adjacent site on the inner surface and in reverse on the outer surface
B. Depolarization of membraneII. Membrane becomes freely permeable to sodium ions, leading to rapid sodium influx
C. Local circuit current flowIII. Outward diffusion of potassium ions restores the resting electrical potential
D. Repolarization of membraneIV. Reversal of polarity occurs, making the inner surface positive and outer surface negative

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nerve impulse conduction operates via a sequence of rapid transient membrane permeability changes, generating localized action potentials propagated by local electrical circuits.

Step 2: Pairing for stimulus application at excited site
When a threshold stimulus is applied to a resting site on the axonal lemma, the membrane becomes suddenly and freely permeable to sodium ions, initiating rapid sodium influx.

Step 3: Pairing for depolarization of membrane
The substantial entry of positively charged sodium ions reverses the electrical polarity, rendering the inner membrane surface positive and the outer surface negative.

Step 4: Pairing for local circuit current flow
Current completes an electrical loop by flowing on the inner surface from the excited site to the adjacent resting site ahead, and returning on the outer surface from the adjacent site back to the excited site.

Step 5: Pairing for repolarization of membrane
Rapid inactivation of sodium channels followed by outward diffusion of potassium ions removes positive charge from the interior, restoring the negative resting potential.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The correct conceptual correspondence pairs stimulus application with rapid sodium permeability, depolarization with polarity reversal, local current flow with inner forward and outer return circuits, and repolarization with outward potassium diffusion restoring the resting potential.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q07 - Synaptic structures and chemical transmission elements

questiontext.text:
Match the junctional features of synapses in List-I with their characteristic properties in List-II:

List-I List-II
A. Electrical synapseI. Fluid-filled space separating the pre-synaptic and post-synaptic membranes
B. Chemical synapseII. Utilizes neurotransmitters; membranes are separated by a cleft and transmission is slower
C. Synaptic cleftIII. Membranes are in close proximity allowing direct current flow; rare in human body
D. Post-synaptic receptorsIV. Specific membrane proteins that bind neurotransmitters to open ion channels

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Synapses are specialized communicative junctions between adjacent neurons classified structurally and functionally into direct electrical synapses and indirect chemical synapses.

Step 2: Pairing for electrical synapse
Electrical synapses have pre- and post-synaptic membranes in extremely close physical apposition, allowing direct ionic current passage; they conduct faster and are rare in the human neural system.

Step 3: Pairing for chemical synapse
Chemical synapses utilize chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) released into a separating cleft, making transmission unidirectional and comparatively slower due to synaptic delay.

Step 4: Pairing for synaptic cleft
The synaptic cleft is the narrow, fluid-filled extracellular space separating the pre-synaptic terminal from the post-synaptic membrane at chemical synapses.

Step 5: Pairing for post-synaptic receptors
Post-synaptic receptors are specialized transmembrane proteins that specifically bind released neurotransmitters, opening ligand-gated ion channels to generate new potentials.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The correct conceptual correspondence pairs electrical synapses with close membrane proximity and rare occurrence, chemical synapses with neurotransmitter mediation across a cleft, synaptic cleft with the separating fluid-filled space, and post-synaptic receptors with neurotransmitter-binding proteins that open ion channels.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q08 - Protective coverings and cerebral hemisphere connections

questiontext.text:
Match the anatomical structures of the human brain coverings and forebrain in List-I with their descriptions in List-II:

List-I List-II
A. Dura materI. Tract of nerve fibres connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres
B. ArachnoidII. Delicate, very thin middle cranial meningeal layer
C. Pia materIII. Outer tough cranial meningeal layer underlying the skull
D. Corpus callosumIV. Innermost cranial meningeal layer in direct contact with brain tissue

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human brain is protected within the cranium by three meningeal envelopes and features specialized white matter commissures that structurally and functionally unite the cerebral hemispheres.

Step 2: Pairing for dura mater
The dura mater is the tough, fibrous, outermost layer of the cranial meninges located immediately beneath the cranial bones.

Step 3: Pairing for arachnoid
The arachnoid mater is the very thin, delicate, web-like intermediate meningeal layer situated between the dura mater and pia mater.

Step 4: Pairing for pia mater
The pia mater is the innermost, highly vascularized meningeal membrane adhering intimately to the contours and sulci of the brain tissue.

Step 5: Pairing for corpus callosum
The corpus callosum is a prominent, thick tract of myelinated nerve fibres that spans the longitudinal cerebral fissure, interconnecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The correct conceptual correspondence pairs dura mater with the tough outer meningeal layer, arachnoid with the very thin middle layer, pia mater with the innermost layer in contact with brain tissue, and corpus callosum with the commissural tract connecting the cerebral hemispheres.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q09 - Functional specializations of cerebral diencephalic regions

questiontext.text:
Match the forebrain regions in List-I with their specialized physiological functions in List-II:

List-I List-II
A. Association areasI. Complex functions like intersensory associations, memory, and communication
B. ThalamusII. Major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signaling
C. HypothalamusIII. Regulates body temperature, urge for eating and drinking, and hormone secretion
D. Limbic systemIV. Regulates sexual behaviour, emotional reactions (pleasure, rage, fear), and motivation

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The forebrain integrates higher cognitive faculties, sensory-motor routing, primary homeostatic drives, and affective emotional states across distinct cortical, thalamic, hypothalamic, and limbic structures.

Step 2: Pairing for association areas
Cortical association areas are regions that are neither clearly sensory nor motor, mediating multi-modal integration responsible for memory, intersensory associations, and communication.

Step 3: Pairing for thalamus
The thalamus is wrapped by the cerebrum and functions as the primary relay and coordinating gatekeeper through which sensory and motor signaling is channeled.

Step 4: Pairing for hypothalamus
Situated at the base of the thalamus, the hypothalamus contains centres governing thermoregulation, hunger, and thirst, as well as neurosecretory cells producing hypothalamic hormones.

Step 5: Pairing for limbic system
Comprising inner cerebral margins, amygdala, and hippocampus, the limbic system interacts with the hypothalamus to govern motivation, sexual behaviour, and emotional expressions including rage, fear, and pleasure.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The correct conceptual correspondence pairs association areas with memory and intersensory associations, thalamus with sensory and motor signal coordination, hypothalamus with body temperature, hunger, and endocrine secretion, and limbic system with emotional expression, motivation, and sexual behaviour.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q10 - Anatomy and physiology of hindbrain structures

Match the brain structures in List-I with their anatomical features and reflex centres in List-II:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The midbrain and hindbrain house essential conduits and coordinating reflex centres controlling autonomic survival mechanisms, motor precision, and inter-regional neural communication.

Step 2: Pairing for corpora quadrigemina
The dorsal aspect of the midbrain features four distinct rounded optic and auditory collicular swellings collectively known as the corpora quadrigemina.

Step 3: Pairing for pons
The pons is a hindbrain bridge consisting of transverse and longitudinal white matter tracts that interconnect disparate regions of the brain.

Step 4: Pairing for cerebellum
The cerebellum possesses an intensely folded, convoluted surface (folia) designed to maximize cortical surface area for millions of coordinating motor neurons.

Step 5: Pairing for medulla oblongata
The medulla oblongata connects to the spinal cord and houses vital autonomic centres governing cardiac rhythms, vascular tone, respiratory rate, and gastric secretions.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The correct conceptual correspondence pairs corpora quadrigemina with the four dorsal midbrain swellings, pons with interconnecting fibre tracts, cerebellum with a convoluted surface accommodating neurons, and medulla oblongata with centres controlling respiration, cardiovascular reflexes, and gastric secretions.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Generation and propagation of axonal nerve impulse

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following physiological events occurring during the generation and conduction of an action potential along an axon in the correct chronological sequence:

(I) Application of a threshold stimulus at a localized site on the polarized axonal membrane

(II) Rapid influx of sodium ions \(\left(\text{Na}^{+}\right)\) into the axoplasm due to increased membrane permeability

(III) Reversal of electrical polarity across the membrane, generating an action potential (depolarization)

(IV) Local current flows from the excited site to the adjacent unexcited site on the inner axonal surface

(V) Outward diffusion of potassium ions \(\left(\text{K}^{+}\\right)\), restoring the resting potential (repolarization)

Choose the correct sequence from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Conduction of a nerve impulse is a sequential electrophysiological process involving localized stimulus-gated membrane activation, sodium-driven depolarization, local circuit propagation, and potassium-mediated repolarization.

Step 2: Initial event - stimulus delivery
The sequence begins when a mechanical, electrical, or chemical stimulus of threshold strength is applied to a resting, polarized site on the axonal lemma.

Step 3: Second event - sodium channel activation and influx
Stimulation immediately triggers the opening of voltage-sensitive sodium channels, dramatically increasing sodium permeability and driving a rapid inward surge of sodium ions into the axoplasm down their electrochemical gradient.

Step 4: Third event - polarity reversal and action potential generation
The massive influx of positive charge overcomes internal resting electronegativity, reversing the transmembrane electrical potential so that the outer surface becomes negative and the inner face becomes positive, producing an action potential (depolarization).

Step 5: Fourth event - local circuit current flow
With the excited site internally positive and the downstream adjacent resting site internally negative, local electrical current flows along the inner surface from the excited site toward the adjacent site, depolarizing the adjacent membrane segment ahead.

Step 6: Fifth event - potassium efflux and repolarization
Sodium channel activation ceases within fractions of a millisecond as channels inactivate; opening of potassium channels allows potassium ions to diffuse outward into the extracellular fluid, rapidly restoring the negative resting potential at the excited site.

Step 7: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological progression proceeds from stimulus application, followed by rapid sodium influx, subsequent reversal of polarity, local current flow to the adjacent site, and concluding with outward potassium diffusion that restores the resting potential.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Sequence of events in chemical synaptic transmission

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following sequential stages of impulse transmission across a chemical synapse in the correct chronological order:

(I) Arrival of an action potential at the pre-synaptic axon terminal

(II) Stimulation of synaptic vesicles to translocate toward the pre-synaptic membrane

(III) Fusion of synaptic vesicles with the pre-synaptic membrane and exocytotic release of neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft

(IV) Diffusion of neurotransmitter molecules across the synaptic cleft and binding to specific receptors on the post-synaptic membrane

(V) Opening of post-synaptic ion channels allowing entry of ions that generate a new graded potential

Choose the correct sequence from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chemical synaptic transmission converts an incoming electrical nerve impulse into a quantized chemical message that traverses the synaptic cleft to generate a subsequent electrical response in the post-synaptic neuron.

Step 2: Initial event - arrival of action potential
The signaling sequence initiates when a conducted action potential arrives at the distal axon terminal of the pre-synaptic neuron, depolarizing the terminal arborization.

Step 3: Second event - vesicle translocation
Terminal depolarization mobilizes neurotransmitter-filled synaptic vesicles, stimulating their directed migration toward the active release zones of the pre-synaptic plasma membrane.

Step 4: Third event - vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release
Synaptic vesicles fuse directly with the pre-synaptic plasma membrane, discharging their chemical neurotransmitters into the extracellular fluid of the synaptic cleft via exocytosis.

Step 5: Fourth event - cleft diffusion and receptor binding
Free neurotransmitter molecules rapidly diffuse across the fluid-filled synaptic cleft and bind specifically to complementary ligand-gated receptor complexes embedded in the post-synaptic membrane.

Step 6: Fifth event - post-synaptic ion channel opening and potential development
Neurotransmitter-receptor binding induces conformational gating of post-synaptic ion channels, permitting specific ionic fluxes that alter the membrane potential, establishing a new excitatory or inhibitory post-synaptic potential.

Step 7: Final Conclusion
The correct physiological sequence proceeds from the arrival of the action potential at the terminal, to vesicle movement toward the membrane, exocytotic neurotransmitter release into the cleft, receptor binding on the post-synaptic membrane, and culminating in ion channel gating that generates a new post-synaptic potential.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q01 - Definition of coordination in human organ systems

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Coordination is an essential physiological process required to maintain homeostasis within the living body.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
According to human physiology, coordination is defined as the process through which two or more organs interact and complement the functions of one another, ensuring that various organ systems work in a synchronized manner.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, coordination involves organs interacting and complementing the functions of one another.

Therefore, the correct answer is: The process through which two or more organs interact and complement the functions of one another.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q02 - Physiological responses of body during physical exercise

questiontext.text: During vigorous physical exercise, which of the following coordinated physiological responses occurs to meet the increased energy demand?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Physical exercise significantly escalates cellular metabolism and energy consumption in skeletal muscles.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
To supply sufficient oxygen for elevated muscular activity, the body coordinates an increase in the rate of respiration, heart beat, and blood flow through the blood vessels. When exercise ceases, these activities gradually return to baseline.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, physical exercise results in an increase in the rate of respiration, heart beat, and blood flow via blood vessels.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Increase in rate of respiration, heart beat, and blood flow via blood vessels.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q03 - Comparison between neural system and endocrine system

generalfeedback.text:

Homeostasis requires two complementary communication networks: the neural system and the endocrine system.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
The neural system provides an organized network of point-to-point connections specialized for quick, immediate coordination. The endocrine system provides chemical integration across tissues and organs through hormones circulating in the bloodstream.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Consequently, the neural system provides point-to-point rapid connections, whereas the endocrine system provides chemical integration through hormones.

Therefore, the correct answer is: The neural system provides point-to-point rapid connections, whereas the endocrine system provides chemical integration through hormones.

answer.text: The neural system acts solely through slow-acting chemicals, whereas the endocrine system uses direct electrical connections

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q07 - Primary anatomical divisions of human neural system

Anatomically, the human neural architecture is organized into two primary divisions.

The two primary divisions are the central neural system (CNS), comprising the brain and spinal cord, and the peripheral neural system (PNS), comprising all the nerves associated with the CNS.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the human neural system consists of the central neural system and the peripheral neural system.

Peripheral nerve fibres are classified based on the direction of impulse conduction relative to the central neural system.

Afferent (sensory) nerve fibres conduct sensory impulses centripetally from peripheral receptors, tissues, and organs toward the CNS for processing. In contrast, efferent fibres carry regulatory impulses away from the CNS to peripheral effectors.

Step 3: Final Conclusion

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q09 - Functional distinction between somatic and autonomic systems

The somatic neural system conveys motor impulses from the CNS to voluntary effectors, specifically skeletal muscles. The autonomic neural system transmits regulatory impulses from the CNS to involuntary organs, cardiac muscle, and smooth muscles.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the somatic system relays impulses to skeletal muscles, whereas the autonomic system transmits impulses to involuntary organs and smooth muscles.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q21 - Comparison between myelinated and non myelinated nerve fibres

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q22 - Differential permeability of resting axonal neural membrane

questiontext.text: When a neuron is in a resting state (not conducting any impulse), its axonal membrane is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The resting axonal membrane exhibits selective ionic permeability determined by resting leakage channels.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
In a resting axon, potassium leak channels remain open, making the membrane comparatively more permeable to potassium ions (\(\text{K}^+\)). Concurrently, voltage-gated sodium channels are closed, making the membrane nearly impermeable to sodium ions (\(\text{Na}^+\)). The membrane is also impermeable to large negatively charged intracellular proteins.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the resting axonal membrane is comparatively more permeable to \(\text{K}^+\) and nearly impermeable to \(\text{Na}^+\).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Comparatively more permeable to \(\text{K}^+\) and nearly impermeable to \(\text{Na}^+\).

Therefore, the correct answer is: High concentration of \(\text{K}^+\) and negatively charged proteins, and low concentration of \(\text{Na}^+\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q24 - Stoichiometry of sodium potassium pump in axons

questiontext.text: The ionic gradients across the resting neural membrane are maintained by the sodium-potassium pump, which transports:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Passive ion leaks across the neural membrane would erode concentration gradients if not counteracted by active transport.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
The sodium-potassium pump (\(\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+\) ATPase) utilizes energy from ATP to actively transport \(3\text{ Na}^+\) ions outwards into the extracellular fluid in exchange for moving \(2\text{ K}^+\) ions inwards into the axoplasm.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q25 - Electrical charge distribution across resting axonal membrane

generalfeedback.text:

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
Because \(3\text{ Na}^+\) are expelled for every \(2\text{ K}^+\) imported, and because non-permeable protein anions reside inside the axoplasm, a net positive charge accumulates on the outer surface while the inner surface remains negatively charged.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q27 - Ionic mechanism of depolarisation upon threshold stimulus

questiontext.text: When a threshold stimulus is applied to a specific site on a polarized axonal membrane, what immediate ionic event initiates depolarization?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Depolarization is an active, voltage-dependent phenomenon driven by rapid changes in membrane permeability.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
Upon application of a threshold stimulus, voltage-gated sodium channels at the site of excitation open rapidly, rendering the membrane freely permeable to sodium ions. Driven by both concentration and electrical gradients, \(\text{Na}^+\) rushes into the axoplasm, resulting in rapid depolarization.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, depolarization is initiated when the membrane becomes freely permeable to \(\text{Na}^+\), causing a rapid influx of \(\text{Na}^+\).

Therefore, the correct answer is: The membrane becomes freely permeable to \(\text{Na}^+\), leading to a rapid influx of \(\text{Na}^+\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q28 - Reversal of membrane polarity during action potential

questiontext.text: During the generation of an action potential at an excited site of an axonal membrane, the reversal of polarity results in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An action potential represents a transient, self-propagating electrical event characterized by polarity reversal.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
The rapid influx of positively charged \(\text{Na}^+\) ions neutralizes internal negative charges and overshoots, making the interior of the axon positive relative to the exterior. Consequently, the outer surface becomes negatively charged while the inner surface becomes positively charged.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the polarity reverses such that the outer surface becomes negatively charged and the inner surface becomes positively charged.

Therefore, the correct answer is: The outer surface becoming negatively charged and the inner surface becoming positively charged.

answer.text: Both the outer and inner surfaces becoming equally positively charged
The outer surface remaining positively charged while the inner surface becomes neutral
The inner surface becoming negatively charged and the outer surface becoming positively charged
The outer surface becoming negatively charged and the inner surface becoming positively charged

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q29 - Local circuit current flow during impulse conduction

questiontext.text: During impulse conduction along an axon from a depolarized site A to an immediately adjacent polarized site B, how does local current flow to complete the circuit?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Local electrical circuits drive the propagation of an action potential along an unmyelinated axonal membrane.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
At depolarized site A, the inner surface is positively charged and the outer surface is negatively charged. At resting site B immediately ahead, the inner surface is negative and outer surface is positive. By physical convention, current flows from positive to negative: on the inner surface, current flows from A to B; on the outer surface, current flows from B to A to complete the closed electrical circuit.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, current flows on the inner surface from site A to site B, and on the outer surface from site B to site A.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Current flows on the inner surface from site A to site B, and on the outer surface from site B to site A.

answer.text: Current flows on the inner surface from site A to site B, and on the outer surface from site B to site A
Current flows on the inner surface from site B to site A, and on the outer surface from site A to site B
Current flows from site A to site B simultaneously across both inner and outer surfaces
Current flows from site B to site A simultaneously across both inner and outer surfaces

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q30 - Mechanisms responsible for repolarisation of axonal membrane

questiontext.text: Following excitation and depolarization, the resting potential of the axonal membrane is restored at the site of stimulation primarily because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Repolarization restores the resting electrical polarity across the excited patch of axonal membrane.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
The stimulus-induced elevation in \(\text{Na}^+\) permeability is extremely transient and rapidly inactivates. It is immediately succeeded by the opening of voltage-gated \(\text{K}^+\) channels. Within a fraction of a second, \(\text{K}^+\) diffuses outwards into the extracellular fluid down its chemical gradient, returning the interior to a negative potential and repolarizing the membrane.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, repolarization occurs because the short-lived rise in \(\text{Na}^+\) permeability is quickly followed by an increase in \(\text{K}^+\) permeability and outward diffusion of \(\text{K}^+\).

Therefore, the correct answer is: The rise in \(\text{Na}^+\) permeability is short-lived and quickly followed by an increase in \(\text{K}^+\) permeability, allowing \(\text{K}^+\) to diffuse outwards.

answer.text: Voltage-gated \(\text{Na}^+\) channels remain open continuously while the \(\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+\) pump shuts down completely
The rise in \(\text{Na}^+\) permeability is short-lived and quickly followed by an increase in \(\text{K}^+\) permeability, allowing \(\text{K}^+\) to diffuse outwards
Intracellular protein anions diffuse out of the membrane down their electrochemical gradient
Extracellular calcium ions enter the cell and neutralize intracellular sodium ions

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q31 - Sequence of events during nerve impulse conduction

questiontext.text: During the generation and conduction of a nerve impulse along an axon, which of the following represents the correct sequence of events following the application of a threshold stimulus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nerve impulse propagation proceeds via a tightly regulated chronological cascade of ionic and electrical events.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
Upon application of a threshold stimulus, voltage-gated \(\text{Na}^+\) channels open, causing a rapid influx of \(\text{Na}^+\). This leads to depolarization and reversal of membrane polarity at site A (action potential). The potential difference between site A and adjacent resting site B drives local current flow on the inner surface from A to B. Finally, \(\text{Na}^+\) channels close and \(\text{K}^+\) diffuses outwards to restore the resting membrane potential.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the sequence is rapid influx of \(\text{Na}^+\), followed by reversal of membrane polarity, local current flow on the inner surface from site A to B, and outward diffusion of \(\text{K}^+\).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Rapid influx of \(\text{Na}^+\) \(\rightarrow\) reversal of membrane polarity \(\rightarrow\) local current flow on inner surface from site A to B \(\rightarrow\) outward diffusion of \(\text{K}^+\).

answer.text: Outward diffusion of \(\text{K}^+\) \(\rightarrow\) local current flow on outer surface \(\rightarrow\) rapid influx of \(\text{Na}^+\) \(\rightarrow\) membrane hyperpolarization
Local current flow on inner surface \(\rightarrow\) outward diffusion of \(\text{K}^+\) \(\rightarrow\) rapid influx of \(\text{Na}^+\) \(\rightarrow\) restoration of resting potential
Rapid influx of \(\text{Na}^+\) \(\rightarrow\) reversal of membrane polarity \(\rightarrow\) local current flow on inner surface from site A to B \(\rightarrow\) outward diffusion of \(\text{K}^+\)
Rapid influx of \(\text{K}^+\) \(\rightarrow\) outward diffusion of \(\text{Na}^+\) \(\rightarrow\) reversal of membrane polarity \(\rightarrow\) local current flow on outer surface

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q32 - Structural boundaries that define a neuronal synapse

questiontext.text: Anatomically, a synapse is formed by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A synapse is the specialized functional junction mediating communication between two consecutive neurons.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
A synapse is formed by the apposition of the pre-synaptic membrane of the transmitting neuron and the post-synaptic membrane of the receiving neuron. Depending on the type of synapse, these membranes may be separated by a fluid-filled synaptic cleft or lie in extremely close proximity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, a synapse is formed by pre-synaptic and post-synaptic membranes, which may or may not be separated by a synaptic cleft.

Therefore, the correct answer is: The membranes of a pre-synaptic neuron and a post-synaptic neuron, which may or may not be separated by a synaptic cleft.

answer.text: The axon hillock and the dendrite of the same neuron separated by a myelin sheath
Two adjacent Schwann cells separated by a node of Ranvier
The neuronal cell body and Nissl's granules connected by neurofibrils
The membranes of a pre-synaptic neuron and a post-synaptic neuron, which may or may not be separated by a synaptic cleft

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q33 - Functional characteristics of electrical synapses in humans

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements regarding electrical synapses in the human neural system is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrical synapses provide direct electrotonic coupling between excitable cells.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
At electrical synapses, pre- and post-synaptic membranes are in very close proximity, allowing electrical current to pass directly from one cell to the other. Because transmission is direct and uninterrupted, it is always faster than chemical transmission; however, electrical synapses are rare in the human nervous system.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, electrical synapses have membranes in very close proximity, allow direct current flow, and are rare in our system.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Pre- and post-synaptic membranes are in very close proximity, allowing direct current flow, but they are rare in our system.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q34 - Sequence of events during chemical synaptic transmission

questiontext.text: At a chemical synapse, what event occurs when an action potential arrives at the axon terminal?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Action potentials trigger exocytosis of neurotransmitters at chemical synapses.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
When an action potential arrives at the pre-synaptic axon terminal, the resulting depolarization stimulates the mobilization of synaptic vesicles toward the active zones of the pre-synaptic plasma membrane. The vesicles fuse with the membrane and discharge their contained neurotransmitters into the fluid-filled synaptic cleft via exocytosis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the arrival of an action potential stimulates synaptic vesicles to move, fuse with the pre-synaptic membrane, and release neurotransmitters into the cleft.

Therefore, the correct answer is: It stimulates synaptic vesicles to move toward the pre-synaptic membrane, fuse with it, and release neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft.

answer.text: It stimulates the post-synaptic membrane to release neurotransmitters backward into the axoplasm
It stimulates synaptic vesicles to move toward the pre-synaptic membrane, fuse with it, and release neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft
It destroys the synaptic cleft, converting the chemical synapse permanently into an electrical synapse
It causes immediate endocytosis of intact neurotransmitter vesicles across the post-synaptic membrane

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q35 - Mechanism of post synaptic potential generation

questiontext.text: How does the release of neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft lead to the generation of a new potential in the post-synaptic neuron?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chemical transmission converts a chemical signal back into an electrical response in the post-synaptic cell.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
Neurotransmitter molecules diffuse across the synaptic cleft and bind specifically to receptor proteins on the post-synaptic membrane. This receptor-ligand interaction causes conformational opening of ligand-gated ion channels, permitting the entry of specific ions that generate a new post-synaptic potential (which may be excitatory or inhibitory).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, neurotransmitters bind specific receptors on the post-synaptic membrane, opening ion channels that permit ion entry.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Neurotransmitters bind to specific receptors on the post-synaptic membrane, opening ion channels that allow ion entry.

answer.text: Neurotransmitters enter the post-synaptic cytoplasm and directly phosphorylate ATP synthase enzymes
Neurotransmitters bind to pre-synaptic receptors that convert electrical current into mechanical tension

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q36 - Comparison between chemical and electrical synaptic speeds

questiontext.text: Why is nerve impulse transmission across an electrical synapse always faster than that across a chemical synapse?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Synaptic delay is an inherent property of chemical synapses due to multi-step biochemical processes.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
Chemical synapses require vesicle trafficking, membrane fusion, exocytosis, diffusion across the synaptic cleft, and receptor binding, introducing a measurable delay. In contrast, electrical synapses possess direct physical continuity via gap junctions, allowing ionic current to flow immediately without synaptic delay.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, electrical synapses are faster because current flows directly from one neuron into another without the delay of chemical transmitter release and diffusion.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Electrical current flows directly from one neuron to another without the delay of chemical transmitter release and diffusion.

answer.text: Electrical synapses are surrounded by thicker myelin sheaths that permit faster saltatory conduction

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q37 - Sequential arrangement of cranial meninges in humans

questiontext.text: From the outside (beneath the skull) to the inside, the cranial meninges protecting the human brain are arranged in which order?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The central nervous system is enveloped by three concentric protective cranial meninges.

Step 2: Application and Evaluation
From the external surface adjacent to the skull to the internal surface contacting brain tissue, the order of the meninges is: outer tough dura mater, middle very thin web-like arachnoid, and inner delicate pia mater.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the order from outside to inside is dura mater, arachnoid, and pia mater.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Dura mater \(\rightarrow\) Arachnoid \(\rightarrow\) Pia mater.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q09 - Axoplasmic composition and sodium potassium pump activity

The statement detailing the axoplasmic composition is accurate because resting axoplasm has high potassium, high protein anions, and low sodium. The statement describing the sodium-potassium pump is also accurate because it actively exports three sodium ions for every two potassium ions imported.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both statements are correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q01 - Basic neural organization in lower organisms

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding the neural organization and coordination in animals:

Statement I: Coordination is the process through which two or more organs interact and complement the functions of one another to maintain homeostasis.

Statement II: In Hydra, the neural organisation is very simple and consists of a network of neurons.

Statement III: In insects, the neural system consists of a completely decentralized nerve net that lacks any brain or ganglia.

Choose the correct option from the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Coordination ensures that multiple physiological systems interact seamlessly to preserve the internal balance (homeostasis) of an organism. Across animal phyla, nervous systems exhibit an evolutionary gradient in complexity from diffuse nets in cnidarians to centralized ganglia in arthropods and highly differentiated brains in vertebrates.

Step 2: Analysis of the proposition regarding coordination
The definition of coordination explicitly states that it is the physiological process through which two or more bodily organs interact and complement each other's functions to maintain homeostasis. Hence, this physiological description is factually accurate.

Step 3: Analysis of the proposition regarding Hydra
Lower invertebrates such as cnidarians (represented by Hydra) exhibit an uncentralized, primitive neural organisation consisting entirely of a network or nerve net of neurons. Hence, this structural characterization is factually accurate.

Step 4: Analysis of the proposition regarding insects
In insects, the neural system is better organized than in cnidarians; it possesses a distinct brain accompanied by segmented ganglia and specialized neural tissues rather than an undifferentiated decentralized net. Hence, this anatomical claim is incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Among the evaluated assertions, the statements describing organ coordination and the nerve network of Hydra are correct, whereas the statement asserting that insects lack a brain and ganglia is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect.
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect.
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect.
Statements I, II, and III are all correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q02 - Functional divisions of peripheral neural system

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding the human peripheral neural system (PNS):

Statement I: Afferent nerve fibres transmit regulatory impulses from the central neural system to peripheral effector tissues and organs.

Statement II: The somatic neural system relays regulatory impulses from the central neural system to skeletal muscles.

Statement III: The autonomic neural system transmits regulatory impulses from the central neural system to involuntary organs and smooth muscles.

Choose the correct option from the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human peripheral neural system comprises afferent (sensory) and efferent (motor) nerve fibres, functionally divided into somatic pathways targeting voluntary skeletal effectors and autonomic pathways targeting visceral involuntary effectors.

Step 2: Analysis of the proposition regarding afferent fibres
Afferent nerve fibres conduct sensory impulses inward from peripheral tissues and sensory organs to the central neural system, whereas efferent fibres carry regulatory or motor commands away from the central neural system to peripheral tissues. Hence, describing afferent fibres as carrying regulatory commands outward is incorrect.

Step 3: Analysis of the proposition regarding the somatic neural system
The somatic neural system is the voluntary division of the peripheral neural system dedicated to relaying impulses from the central neural system directly to skeletal muscles. Hence, this functional assignment is factually accurate.

Step 4: Analysis of the proposition regarding the autonomic neural system
The autonomic neural system manages involuntary functions by relaying impulses from the central neural system to smooth muscles, cardiac tissue, and visceral involuntary organs. Hence, this functional assignment is factually accurate.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Among the evaluated assertions, the statements concerning the somatic neural system and autonomic neural system are correct, whereas the statement concerning the direction of transmission in afferent nerve fibres is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect.
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect.
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect.
Statements I, II, and III are all correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q03 - Morphological parts and organelles of neurons

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding the structure of a human neuron:

Statement I: Nissl's granules are granular bodies composed of organelles that are abundantly distributed throughout the cell body and the entire length of the axon.

Statement II: Dendrites are short, repeatedly branching projections that conduct nerve impulses away from the cell body toward downstream synapses.

Statement III: Each axon terminates in fine branches with bulb-like synaptic knobs that contain synaptic vesicles filled with neurotransmitters.

Choose the correct option from the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A typical neuron comprises three distinct structural zones: the cell body (soma), receptive branched dendrites, and an elongated conducting axon terminating in secretory synaptic knobs.

Step 2: Analysis of the proposition regarding Nissl's granules
Nissl's granules (composed of rough endoplasmic reticulum and ribosomes) are characteristically found in the cell body and dendrites of a neuron, but they are strictly absent from the axoplasm of the axon. Hence, claiming that they are distributed along the entire length of the axon is incorrect.

Step 3: Analysis of the proposition regarding dendrites
Dendrites are receptive processes that transmit electrical impulses toward the cell body, whereas the axon is responsible for conducting nerve impulses away from the cell body. Hence, asserting that dendrites conduct impulses away from the cell body is incorrect.

Step 4: Analysis of the proposition regarding synaptic knobs
The distal arborization of an axon forms terminal bulb-like swellings known as synaptic knobs, which house synaptic vesicles loaded with chemical neurotransmitters. Hence, this structural description is factually accurate.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Among the evaluated assertions, only the statement describing the axon terminals and synaptic knobs is correct, while the statements concerning the axonal distribution of Nissl's granules and dendrite conduction direction are incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect.
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect.
Only Statement III is correct, while Statements I and II are incorrect.
Statements I, II, and III are all correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q04 - Classification of neurons by process count

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding the structural types of neurons:

Statement I: Multipolar neurons have one axon and two or more dendrites and are prominently found in the cerebral cortex.

Statement II: Bipolar neurons possess one axon and one dendrite and are characteristically located in the retina of the eye.

Statement III: Unipolar neurons possess a cell body with only a single axon and are typically found during the embryonic stage.

Choose the correct option from the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Neurons are classified morphologically based on the number of processes extending from the soma into multipolar, bipolar, and unipolar categories, each adapted to specific anatomical locations.

Step 2: Analysis of the proposition regarding multipolar neurons
Multipolar neurons possess a single axon along with two or more branching dendrites; this configuration constitutes the predominant neuronal morphology found within the cerebral cortex. Hence, this structural description is factually accurate.

Step 3: Analysis of the proposition regarding bipolar neurons
Bipolar neurons are specialized sensory neurons that feature precisely one dendrite and one axon arising from opposite poles of the cell body, commonly found in the retina of the eye. Hence, this histological localization is factually accurate.

Step 4: Analysis of the proposition regarding unipolar neurons
Unipolar neurons consist of a soma with only a single emerging axonal process, a pattern predominantly seen during early embryonic developmental stages. Hence, this developmental characterization is factually accurate.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
All three evaluated assertions accurately describe the morphological distinctions and physiological locations of multipolar, bipolar, and unipolar neurons.

answer.text: Only Statement I is correct, while Statements II and III are incorrect.
Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect.
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect.
Statements I, II, and III are all correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q05 - Myelinated versus unmyelinated axonal nerve fibres

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding myelinated and unmyelinated nerve fibres:

Statement I: In myelinated nerve fibres, Schwann cells form a lipid-rich myelin sheath around the axon, leaving periodic unmyelinated gaps called nodes of Ranvier.

Statement II: Myelinated nerve fibres are typically found enclosed within cranial and spinal nerves.

Statement III: Unmyelinated nerve fibres lack Schwann cells altogether and are found exclusively within the white matter of the central neural system.

Choose the correct option from the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Axons in the peripheral and central nervous systems are categorized as myelinated or unmyelinated based on the presence and arrangement of insulating glial sheaths around them.

Step 2: Analysis of the proposition regarding myelinated fibres and nodes of Ranvier
Schwann cells wrap repeatedly around the axon in myelinated peripheral nerve fibres, forming an insulating myelin sheath interrupted at regular intervals by unsheathed gaps called nodes of Ranvier. Hence, this anatomical description is factually accurate.

Step 3: Analysis of the proposition regarding cranial and spinal nerves
Myelinated nerve fibres are the primary constituent of both spinal and cranial nerves, facilitating rapid saltatory conduction. Hence, this anatomical distribution is factually accurate.

Step 4: Analysis of the proposition regarding unmyelinated fibres
An unmyelinated nerve fibre in the peripheral neural system is indeed enclosed by Schwann cells, but these cells do not wrap around the axon to form a myelin sheath; furthermore, unmyelinated fibres are characteristically found in autonomic and somatic neural systems rather than exclusively in central white matter. Hence, this assertion is incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Among the evaluated assertions, the statements detailing the structure of myelinated fibres and their presence in cranial and spinal nerves are correct, whereas the statement claiming unmyelinated fibres completely lack Schwann cells is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect.
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect.
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect.
Statements I, II, and III are all correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q06 - Ionic gradients across resting axonal membrane

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding the resting membrane potential of an axon:

Statement I: In an unexcited, resting neuron, the axonal membrane exhibits significantly higher permeability to potassium ions \(\left(\text{K}^{+}\right)\) than to sodium ions \(\left(\text{Na}^{+}\right)\).

Statement II: Negatively charged intracellular proteins present in the axoplasm freely diffuse outward across the resting axonal membrane along their concentration gradient.

Statement III: The sodium-potassium pump actively transports 3 sodium ions \(\left(\text{Na}^{+}\right)\) outward into extracellular fluid for every 2 potassium ions \(\left(\text{K}^{+}\right)\) inward into the axoplasm.

Choose the correct option from the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The resting membrane potential of an excitable neural cell is established by differential passive ionic permeabilities across the membrane combined with active primary ionic transport.

Step 2: Analysis of the proposition regarding resting permeability to potassium and sodium
In the resting state, passive leakage channels render the axonal membrane comparatively permeable to potassium ions but nearly impermeable to sodium ions. Hence, this physiological description is factually accurate.

Step 3: Analysis of the proposition regarding negatively charged axoplasmic proteins
The axonal membrane is impermeable to the large, negatively charged proteins localized inside the axoplasm, preventing their outward diffusion and contributing to the internal negativity. Hence, claiming that these proteins diffuse freely across the resting membrane is incorrect.

Step 4: Analysis of the proposition regarding the sodium-potassium ATPase pump
The electrogenic sodium-potassium pump consumes ATP to actively transport 3 sodium ions outwards for every 2 potassium ions brought inwards, sustaining the requisite steep chemical gradients. Hence, this stoichiometric description is factually accurate.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Among the evaluated assertions, the statements concerning the selective ionic permeability and the active transport stoichiometry of the sodium-potassium pump are correct, while the statement asserting membrane permeability to axoplasmic proteins is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect.
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect.
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect.
Statements I, II, and III are all correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q07 - Depolarization and local circuit impulse conduction

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding the generation and conduction of an action potential along an axon:

Statement I: Application of a threshold stimulus causes a rapid efflux of sodium ions \(\left(\text{Na}^{+}\right)\) from the axoplasm, leading to hyperpolarization of the membrane.

Statement II: Depolarization results in a reversal of membrane polarity at the stimulated site, making the inner surface positively charged relative to the outer surface.

Statement III: During impulse propagation, local electric current flows on the inner surface from the depolarized site to the adjacent resting site, while flowing in the opposite direction on the outer surface.

Choose the correct option from the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nerve impulse conduction involves localized transient depolarization followed by self-propagating local electrical circuit loops along adjacent segments of the axonal lemma.

Step 2: Analysis of the proposition regarding threshold stimulation and sodium flux
Application of a threshold stimulus increases membrane permeability to sodium, causing a rapid influx (entry into the axoplasm) of sodium ions rather than an efflux, resulting in depolarization rather than hyperpolarization. Hence, this assertion is incorrect.

Step 3: Analysis of the proposition regarding membrane polarity reversal
The rapid influx of positively charged sodium ions reverses the resting potential polarity, turning the inner surface of the axonal membrane positive with respect to its outer surface at the excited locus. Hence, this electrical event is factually accurate.

Step 4: Analysis of the proposition regarding local current flow circuits
At adjacent resting sites, the interior is still negative; thus, current flows internally from the depolarized site to the adjacent resting site, and externally from the resting site back to the depolarized site, completing the local circuit and triggering depolarization ahead. Hence, this local circuit mechanism is factually accurate.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Among the evaluated assertions, the statements describing polarity reversal during depolarization and internal local current flow are correct, whereas the statement claiming sodium efflux occurs upon stimulation is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect.
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect.
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect.
Statements I, II, and III are all correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q08 - Repolarization mechanism of excited axonal membrane

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding the repolarization phase of an action potential in an axon:

Statement I: The stimulus-induced increase in axonal membrane permeability to sodium ions \(\left(\text{Na}^{+}\right)\) is extremely short-lived.

Statement II: The initial rapid influx of sodium ions is quickly followed by an increase in membrane permeability to potassium ions \(\left(\text{K}^{+}\right)\).

Statement III: Outward diffusion of potassium ions across the axonal membrane rapidly restores the original resting electrical potential at the excited site.

Choose the correct option from the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Action potential termination and restoration of the resting membrane potential (repolarization) require rapid time-dependent inactivation of sodium channels coupled with delayed activation of potassium conductance.

Step 2: Analysis of the proposition regarding sodium permeability duration
The opening of voltage-gated sodium channels upon stimulation is transient, and the elevated sodium permeability terminates within a fraction of a millisecond as channels inactivate. Hence, this kinetic description is factually accurate.

Step 3: Analysis of the proposition regarding potassium permeability onset
Immediately following sodium channel inactivation, voltage-sensitive potassium channels open, leading to an elevated membrane permeability specifically to potassium ions. Hence, this sequential transition is factually accurate.

Step 4: Analysis of the proposition regarding restoration of resting potential
As potassium ions diffuse down their electrochemical gradient out of the cell, positive charge exits the axoplasm, restoring the electronegativity of the inner membrane surface back to its resting state. Hence, this physiological restoration is factually accurate.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
All three evaluated assertions accurately reflect the sequential physiological events underlying axonal membrane repolarization.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect.
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect.
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect.
Statements I, II, and III are all correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q09 - Comparative properties of electrical chemical synapses

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding electrical and chemical synapses:

Statement I: Impulse transmission across an electrical synapse is always faster than transmission across a chemical synapse.

Statement II: Electrical synapses are rare in the human neural system compared to chemical synapses.

Statement III: At electrical synapses, pre-synaptic and post-synaptic membranes are separated by a wide, fluid-filled synaptic cleft across which neurotransmitters diffuse.

Choose the correct option from the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Synapses are specialized neuro-junctional structures operating either via direct electrical current continuity through low-resistance channels or via chemical messenger diffusion across an intervening gap.

Step 2: Analysis of the proposition regarding synaptic transmission velocity
Because ionic current flows directly between cells without the delay of vesicle exocytosis, diffusion, and receptor binding, impulse transmission across an electrical synapse is always significantly faster than across a chemical synapse. Hence, this comparative statement is factually accurate.

Step 3: Analysis of the proposition regarding prevalence of electrical synapses
In the human body and mammalian neural systems generally, electrical synapses occur rarely, whereas chemical synapses represent the predominant form of junctional communication. Hence, this anatomical assertion is factually accurate.

Step 4: Analysis of the proposition regarding synaptic cleft at electrical synapses
Electrical synapses feature plasma membranes positioned in extremely close proximity without a prominent fluid-filled synaptic cleft and operate without chemical neurotransmitters; wide fluid-filled clefts and neurotransmitter diffusion are defining hallmarks of chemical synapses. Hence, this morphological claim is incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Among the evaluated assertions, the statements concerning conduction speed and anatomical rarity of electrical synapses are correct, whereas the statement attributing a wide cleft and neurotransmitters to electrical synapses is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect.
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect.
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect.
Statements I, II, and III are all correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q10 - Chemical transmission across synaptic junctions

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding transmission of impulses across a chemical synapse:

Statement I: The arrival of an action potential at the axon terminal stimulates synaptic vesicles to move toward and fuse with the pre-synaptic membrane.

Statement II: Neurotransmitters released into the synaptic cleft bind selectively to receptors located exclusively on the pre-synaptic membrane to trigger exocytosis.

Statement III: Binding of neurotransmitters to post-synaptic receptors opens ion channels, generating a new potential that can be either excitatory or inhibitory.

Choose the correct option from the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chemical synaptic transmission converts an electrical action potential in the presynaptic terminal into a chemical signal that diffuses across the synaptic cleft to generate a graded postsynaptic potential.

Step 2: Analysis of the proposition regarding vesicle exocytosis
When an action potential invades the axon terminal, depolarization triggers synaptic vesicle mobilization, leading to membrane fusion and release of neurotransmitter molecules into the synaptic cleft. Hence, this sequence of events is factually accurate.

Step 3: Analysis of the proposition regarding neurotransmitter receptor localization
Released neurotransmitter molecules bind specifically to receptor proteins situated on the post-synaptic membrane, not on the pre-synaptic membrane, to initiate signal transduction in the receiving neuron. Hence, this receptor localization claim is incorrect.

Step 4: Analysis of the proposition regarding post-synaptic ion channel gating
The binding of ligands to post-synaptic receptors opens ion channels, allowing specific ionic fluxes that alter the membrane potential of the post-synaptic cell, which may be excitatory (depolarizing) or inhibitory (hyperpolarizing). Hence, this electrophysiological outcome is factually accurate.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Among the evaluated assertions, the statements describing vesicle fusion at the pre-synaptic terminal and ion channel opening on the post-synaptic membrane are correct, while the statement regarding pre-synaptic receptor binding is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q11 - Cranial meninges and cerebral hemisphere organization

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding the cranial meninges and cerebral architecture of the human brain:

Statement I: The cranial meninges protecting the brain comprise three layers: an outer fibrous dura mater, a very thin middle arachnoid, and an inner pia mater that contacts brain tissue.

Statement II: The two cerebral hemispheres are structurally connected along the midline by a canal called the cerebral aqueduct.

Statement III: The cerebral cortex appears grey because neuron cell bodies are concentrated there, whereas myelinated nerve fibre tracts give the inner region an opaque white appearance.

Choose the correct option from the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human brain is protected by bony cranium and three meningeal coverings, while its cerebrum displays histological compartmentalization into peripheral cellular grey matter and deep myelinated white matter connected by commissural tracts.

Step 2: Analysis of the proposition regarding cranial meningeal layers
The cranial meninges consist of three concentric layers: the outermost tough dura mater, the thin intermediate arachnoid mater, and the vascular innermost pia mater adhering directly to brain parenchyma. Hence, this anatomical order and description is factually accurate.

Step 3: Analysis of the proposition regarding cerebral hemisphere connectivity
The two cerebral hemispheres are interconnected by a massive transverse tract of nerve fibres called the corpus callosum, whereas the cerebral aqueduct is a narrow canal passing through the midbrain. Hence, identifying the connecting bridge as the cerebral aqueduct is incorrect.

Step 4: Analysis of the proposition regarding grey and white matter histology
The outer cerebral cortex is designated grey matter because it is dense with unmyelinated neuronal cell bodies, while the internal cerebrum forms white matter due to bundles of myelin-sheathed axonal tracts. Hence, this histological distinction is factually accurate.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Among the evaluated assertions, the statements detailing the trilaminar cranial meninges and the histological basis of cortical grey and white matter are correct, whereas the statement identifying the interhemispheric commissure as the cerebral aqueduct is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect.
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_STATEMENT_Q12 - Functional organization of the cerebral cortex

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding functional specialization in the forebrain:

Statement I: The cerebral cortex contains distinct motor areas, sensory areas, and large association areas that are neither clearly sensory nor motor in function.

Statement II: Cortical association areas are responsible for mediating complex cognitive functions including intersensory associations, memory, and communication.

Statement III: The cerebrum wraps around the thalamus, which serves as a major relay and coordinating centre for sensory and motor signaling.

Choose the correct option from the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The forebrain integrates sensory inputs and orchestrates motor outputs via dedicated primary functional cortical regions, high-order multimodal association cortices, and thalamic gating nuclei.

Step 2: Analysis of the proposition regarding cortical functional zones
The cerebral cortex is organized into defined motor strips, sensory receiving areas, and extensive intermediate association zones that lack purely sensory or motor categorization. Hence, this structural-functional categorization is factually accurate.

Step 3: Analysis of the proposition regarding association area functions
Multimodal association areas integrate information from disparate sensory modalities, playing pivotal roles in complex integrative processes like intersensory associations, memory consolidation, and communicative faculties. Hence, this functional delineation is factually accurate.

Step 4: Analysis of the proposition regarding thalamic coordination
The thalamus is wrapped by the cerebral hemispheres and serves as the primary gateway and coordinating station through which sensory and motor pathways are sorted and routed. Hence, this topographical and functional statement is factually accurate.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
All three evaluated assertions accurately characterize the functional subdivisions of the cerebral cortex and the sensory-motor coordinating role of the thalamus.
